strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: partitioning tokens into two groups with sparse attention eliminates MASK tokens entirely, allowing inference to process only unmasked tokens — a genuinely novel architectural perspective on masked generative modeling

Strong and carefully measured inference efficiency gains: ~5-5.5x latency and throughput improvements over MDLM at equal or better generative perplexity, with latency/throughput measured with mean and std over batches on specified hardware

Excellent experimental hygiene: ablations isolate the complementary-masking effect from the architectural effect (Section 5.3), FP64 logit casting follows prior work on precision pitfalls, unigram entropy is reported to detect degenerate generation, and training/inference compute costs are disclosed

Good breadth: experiments on LM1B, OpenWebText, and ImageNet; downstream evaluations on LAMBADA and other lm-eval-harness tasks; compatibility with SDTT distillation is demonstrated with clear speed-quality tradeoffs

Honest limitations section acknowledging the parameter-count inflation needed on OWT, higher training cost, and preliminary image results; code and checkpoints promised for release with detailed hyperparameters in the appendix
weaknesses: On OpenWebText, PGMs with matched depth underperform MDLM on validation perplexity and require a larger model (dim 1024 or more layers) to win, partially confounding the quality comparison; the improved perplexity claims come at higher parameter count and ~75-80% of MDLM's training throughput

Likelihood/theoretical grounding is thin: the paper does not clarify whether the PGM objective is a valid (tight) bound on data log-likelihood in the same sense as MDLM's NELBO, nor formally characterize what generative process the partition-based denoiser defines; the MDLM-equivalence of the sampler is asserted rather than proven

Baseline coverage is narrow: comparisons are essentially limited to MDLM and GPT-2-small; stronger or more recent non-autoregressive alternatives (e.g., Block Diffusion with KV caching, any-order AR models, faster samplers for MDLM) are discussed but not compared empirically

Generative perplexity (GPT-2 Large) as the primary sample-quality metric is known to be gameable, and no human evaluation or diversity metrics beyond unigram entropy are provided; image experiments are preliminary and far from MaskGIT-quality baselines
Single training seed with no error bars on perplexity or downstream accuracy; results differences (e.g., 1.95 PPL on LM1B, ~0.37 PPL on OWT) may be within run-to-run variance

The efficiency claim depends on the specialized architecture (encoder-decoder without decoder self-attention), and the connection between the partitioning scheme and this architecture is not fully disentangled — it remains unclear how much of the speedup would transfer to other PGM variants

strengths: Clear and simple core idea: eliminating MASK tokens by partitioning tokens into two disjoint groups with attention masking, which yields genuine 5x latency/throughput gains at the same number of sampling steps, carefully measured on standard hardware with error bars

Honest and thorough experimental practice: the authors disentangle the effect of complementary masking from the architecture change (Section 5.3), re-run baselines from scratch, use FP64 sampling to avoid the underflow artifact [57], report unigram entropy alongside generative perplexity, and openly acknowledge limitations (need for more parameters, higher training cost, weaker post-distillation results)

Reasonable breadth: text (LM1B, OpenWebText), a preliminary image experiment, downstream benchmarks, and compatibility with SDTT distillation; code and hyperparameters are described in detail and promised for release
weaknesses: The headline quality gains are fragile and partly confounded. On LM1B, the PGM (26.80) actually underperforms the MDLM + complementary masking baseline (25.72), meaning the 1.95 perplexity improvement over vanilla MDLM is largely attributable to complementary masking, not the proposed architecture. On the main long-context benchmark (OWT), PGM with matched size underperforms MDLM (26.96 vs 25.35 at 200k steps) and only wins after increasing parameters (dim 1024 or more layers), so the quality-vs-efficiency comparison is not parameter-matched

No theoretical grounding: the paper borrows the MDLM absorbing-diffusion posterior (Eq. 3) and NELBO weighting, but the model never sees MASK tokens and predictions for a position are constrained to not depend on that position's token. It is unclear whether the resulting sampler corresponds to a valid ELBO of any well-defined generative process, or what approximation gap is introduced; the perplexity gains/losses are therefore hard to interpret

The strongest efficiency claims involve apples-to-oranges comparisons: the 280x improvement is relative to MDLM at 1024 steps (a strawman step count), and the 10.73x win over GPT-2 with KV caching is at a very small model scale (<300M) where the comparison has limited relevance; after SDTT distillation, MDLM+SDTT actually achieves lower generative perplexity than PGM+SDTT at equal latency, undermining the claim that PGM dominates after distillation

The proposed architecture is complex and somewhat ad hoc (encoder with group-wise self-attention, GroupSwap cross-attention layer, data-independent vs data-dependent query initializations, no decoder self-attention), and the design choices are supported only by small-scale ablations; it is unclear how well the mechanism scales, and training is slower due to dense attention masks

Evaluation is limited: only two text datasets at modest scale, single training seeds with no error bars on perplexity metrics, generative perplexity judged by GPT-2 Large with 1,024 samples (a weak and increasingly questioned metric), no human evaluation or modern baselines (e.g., other accelerated discrete diffusion or any-order AR models), and the image results are explicitly preliminary with weaker gains

Novelty is moderate: the contribution is essentially an architectural trick (attention masking + cross-attention decoding) layered on an existing MDLM training/sampling recipe, related to any-order autoregressive and non-AR generation literature, and the distillation component is reused unchanged from prior work

strengths: The core idea is simple, clean, and well-motivated: replacing MASK tokens with a two-group partition with attention masking, which allows the model to process only unmasked tokens at inference and to compute logits only for positions being denoised. This yields a genuine architectural source of inference speedup (5-5.5x latency/throughput over MDLM) rather than relying solely on sampler tricks.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: validation perplexity on LM1B and OpenWebText, generative perplexity with entropy checks to catch degenerate generation, FP64 casting to avoid the known 16-bit underflow artifact, latency/throughput measurements with error bars on a single A100, distillation with SDTT, downstream tasks (LAMBADA, ARC, HellaSwag, etc.), and preliminary ImageNet results.

The paper honestly disentangles the contribution of the architecture from the effect of 'complementary masking' via a controlled MDLM baseline with doubled effective batch size (Section 5.3), which strengthens the empirical claims and reveals where PGM does and does not help (LM1B vs OWT).

Compatibility with SDTT distillation is demonstrated, including an honest analysis showing PGM+SDTT currently underperforms MDLM+SDTT in generative perplexity after distillation (Figure 6, Table 7), plus a careful precision-controlled re-distillation of MDLM for fairness.

Reproducibility is strong: built on the open-source MDLM codebase, full hyperparameters in Appendix A, sampling pseudocode, detailed training/inference costs, and a commitment to release code and checkpoints under MIT license.

Limitations are candidly discussed (Section 8): PGMs require more parameters to match MDLM perplexity at context length 1024, training is ~25% slower, and distillation gains are smaller than for MDLM.
weaknesses: Fairness of the headline comparisons is a concern: the best PGMs (6/6, dim=1024 or 8/8) have more parameters than the MDLM baseline (dim=768), so the 5x latency improvement and better perplexity are not achieved at matched model size. At matched size (PGM 8/8), PGM only marginally beats MDLM on OWT perplexity (25.10 vs 25.35 at 200k; 22.70 vs 23.07 at 1M), and MDLM with complementary masking (22.98) is very close. The efficiency-per-parameter trade-off is not analyzed.

The comparison to GPT-2 Small with KV caching (10.73x latency) is a weak and dated baseline for claims about beating autoregressive inference; stronger/contemporary AR baselines or matched-FLOP comparisons are missing.

No theoretical or formal analysis of the method: it is unclear in what sense the PGM objective relates to a likelihood bound on the data. How validation perplexity is computed for PGM (the weighted loss is not obviously a NELBO in the MDLM sense) is not precisely specified, making perplexity comparisons with MDLM methodologically murky.

After distillation, PGM+SDTT produces notably worse generative perplexity than MDLM+SDTT (e.g., 72.19 vs 56.34 at 32 steps), weakening the overall story that PGMs dominate; the paper attributes this to architecture immaturity but offers no diagnosis.
The gains on images are preliminary and smaller, evaluated at small scale and short sequence length; generalization beyond text remains unproven, and the authors defer this to future work.

No error bars over training seeds for perplexity results (acknowledged), and the ablation space (encoder/decoder splits, query initializations) is explored mainly at 200k steps, so conclusions about the best configuration may be unstable at 1M steps.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: replacing [MASK] tokens with a two-partition scheme with constrained (group-sparse) attention, which removes the wasted computation on masked tokens at inference while preserving parallel, any-order decoding of MGMs.

Sound technical treatment: the Partition Transformer (partition-wise encoder, GroupSwap cross-attention layer, cross-attention-only decoder) is carefully designed to prevent information leakage between partitions, and the paper is explicit about why a standard bidirectional transformer cannot be used (Sec. 3/4).

Comprehensive evaluation across two modalities: language modeling on LM1B and OpenWebText (validation PPL, Generative PPL, unigram entropy, downstream lm-eval tasks) and image generation on ImageNet256 with MaskGIT (FID/IS with both confidence and Halton samplers), plus SDTT distillation compatibility.

Good ablations: the paper isolates the contribution of complementary masking (Sec. 5.3) rather than attributing all gains to the architecture, studies balanced vs. imbalanced encoder/decoder splits and data-dependent vs. independent queries, and analyzes training stability and precision effects (Fig. 5, D.2, D.4).

Honest reporting of limitations: increased parameter count needed to match MDLM perplexity on 1024-token contexts, slower training due to dense sdpa masks, and the gap between PGM and the complementary-masking upper bound are all explicitly acknowledged.

Large practical speedups (5–5.5x on text, ~7.5x on images at matched steps) with near-parity quality metrics, and detailed latency/throughput tables including a longer-context (4096) efficiency study.
weaknesses: Parameter-matched comparisons are weak: on OpenWebText, the best PGMs require 203M–268M parameters vs. MDLM's 170M, so some of the quality and even efficiency gains partly come from a larger model; throughput comparisons should be complemented with matched-parameter or matched-FLOP settings.

The 7.5x ImageNet speedup comes with slightly worse FID at matched steps (5.54 vs. 5.35); the improvement over MaskGIT FID (4.56) requires doubling the sampling steps, so the quality–speed trade-off is less favorable than the headline suggests, and the training was shortened (500k vs. 2M steps), making baseline comparisons imperfect.

No quantitative comparison with closely related hybrid approaches (Eso-LMs, Block Diffusion) despite detailed qualitative discussion in Suppl. B; the claim that PGMs are 'mostly orthogonal' would be more convincing with direct empirical comparison on at least one shared benchmark.

Training is ~20–25% slower than MDLM at the same context length (Table 3), and no efficient kernels for the block-diagonal attention are implemented, so end-to-end wall-clock savings are not yet demonstrated; the impact on overall training-inference cost balance deserves more analysis.

Experiments are limited to context lengths of at most 1024 during training, and the GroupSwap/param-count overhead appears to grow with context length (complementary masking helps less on OWT), raising questions about scalability to modern LLM context lengths.

Some writing/consistency issues (e.g., typos such as 'retaioning', 'while while', a table typo '365.97c', inconsistent throughput formatting in Table 7) and minor ambiguity in the binomial sampling description slightly reduce polish.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: replacing [MASK] tokens with two disjoint partitions constrained by sparse attention, which enables processing only clean tokens during sampling while retaining parallel, any-order generation of MGMs.

The Partition Transformer architecture (encoder, GroupSwap layer, decoder with cross-attention only) is a clean and non-trivial design that provably prevents information leakage between partitions; both data-independent and data-dependent query initializations are explored.

Comprehensive and honest empirical evaluation across text (LM1B, OpenWebText) and images (ImageNet256/MaskGIT), including perplexity, Generative Perplexity, unigram entropy, downstream lm-eval tasks, FID/IS, latency and throughput, with details on numerical precision (FP64 logits) that other works have neglected.

Useful ablations: complementary masking isolated as a factor (Sec. 5.3), balanced vs. imbalanced encoder/decoder layer splits, query initialization variants, longer-context throughput (4096), and distillation compatibility (SDTT) — showing PGMs plug into existing MGM distillation with minor modifications.

Strong headline results: 5–5.5x higher sampling throughput than MDLM with better or comparable perplexity/Gen-PPL, and 7.5x throughput vs. MaskGIT with only a small FID gap (4.56 FID at 2x steps still 3.9x faster).

Transparent limitations section acknowledging the increased parameter count needed to match MDLM at 1024 context, higher training cost due to dense masking in sdpa, and preliminary analysis (Suppl. D.1) of why complementary masking helps at short context.
weaknesses: Comparisons are not parameter- or compute-matched: the best PGMs (268M params) are substantially larger than the MDLM baseline (170M), so part of the perplexity gain and possibly the quality-speed tradeoff comes from extra parameters rather than the partitioning idea alone; the faster PGM 8/8 (203M) also has more parameters than MDLM.

Training is 25–40% more expensive per step than MDLM (Table 3), so end-to-end compute-for-quality efficiency is not clearly improved; the claimed 5x gain is inference-only and relies on an unoptimized baseline attention implementation trade-off (dense sdpa masks) that the authors themselves flag as fixable for PGMs too.

Text sample quality is evaluated mainly via Generative Perplexity (GPT-2-based) and unigram entropy, which are weak and potentially gameable proxies; no human evaluation or AR-baseline (e.g., GPT-2 small trained comparably) quality comparison for text generation.

At matched sampling steps on ImageNet, PGM is slightly worse than MaskGIT with the Halton sampler (5.54 vs. 5.35 FID); the headline FID improvement (4.56) requires 2x the sampling steps, so the quality claim is nuanced despite the abstract's framing.

The complementary-masking ablation reveals the architecture itself may be a bottleneck: MDLM with complementary masking beats PGM on LM1B, and the gain on OWT is small (23.07 → 22.98), suggesting the improvements come partly from the training signal rather than PGM per se; loss spikes observed with complementary masking raise scaling concerns.

Scale of experiments is modest: 170–268M param models, context length limited to 1024 (no trained 4096 models), ImageNet 256x256 only, and ImageNet training reduced to 500k steps vs. 2M for the original baseline; applicability to modern LLM scales is untested.

Several inconsistencies in tables (e.g., duplicated latency/throughput values in Table 7 rows, a typo '365.97c' in Table 9, formatting artifacts like 'retaioning' in the intro and doubled 'while while' in the abstract) suggest the manuscript needed more careful proofreading.
No released code/artifacts at review time (only a promise of MIT-licensed release), which limits reproducibility of the specialized architecture and sampling algorithms.

strengths: The core idea—replacing [MASK] tokens with two disjoint partitions and sparse attention—is clean, well-motivated, and directly addresses a real inefficiency in MGMs (processing full-length sequences during sampling). It preserves parallel/any-order generation while processing only clean tokens at inference, which is an elegant combination of AR and MGM advantages.

Comprehensive and largely convincing empirical evaluation across both language (LM1B, OpenWebText) and image (ImageNet256) domains, with multiple metrics: validation perplexity, generative perplexity with entropy controls, downstream tasks via lm-eval-harness, FID/IS for images, plus latency/throughput measurements. The speedups (5–7.5×) are substantial and reproduced across settings.

Ablations are genuinely useful: balanced encoder/decoder splits, data-dependent vs. data-independent queries, and a careful experiment (Sec. 5.3) that isolates the contribution of complementary masking from the architecture change—this is the right way to disentangle the contributions and shows intellectual honesty.
The paper demonstrates PGMs are compatible with existing distillation methods (SDTT) rather than claiming everything from scratch, and reports throughput even after distillation.

Transparency: limitations are candidly acknowledged (more parameters needed on OWT, slightly higher FID than MaskGIT with Halton, slower training due to dense masks, training loss spikes), and training/inference costs and licensing are reported. This raises confidence in the reported gains.

Efficiency claims are measured carefully (fixed hardware, warmup batches, standard deviations) and cross-checked at longer context (Table 10), and the FP64 logits cast addresses known sampling precision pitfalls (Zheng et al., 2025).
weaknesses: Matching baseline quality on OWT requires a larger model (203M/268M vs. MDLM's 170M) or more layers. The headline throughput comparisons do not fully account for this parameter gap; a matched-parameter or matched-FLOP analysis at inference would strengthen the claims, especially since the throughput advantage is the central selling point.

Training is ~25% slower than MDLM at the same scale (Table 3) due to naive dense masking in sdpa; the paper argues this is fixable with block-diagonal kernels but does not demonstrate it. The method currently trades training cost for inference speed, which should be weighed more prominently.

Scale and baselines are somewhat dated/modest: 170–270M parameters, context length 1024 (4096 only measured for throughput, not trained), and baselines limited to MDLM and MaskGIT. Comparisons against stronger recent discrete diffusion/hybrid models (e.g., Block Diffusion/BD3-LM, Eso-LMs beyond the qualitative discussion) are missing, and it is unclear how PGM scales.

Generative Perplexity computed with GPT-2 Large is a weak and somewhat contested metric for sample quality; the paper correctly adds unigram entropy, but the text-quality evidence remains indirect (no human evaluation or stronger reference-model evaluation).

On ImageNet, the quality story is mixed: PGM slightly trails MaskGIT under the Halton sampler at 32 steps (5.54 vs 5.35) and only wins when doubling steps; the abstract frames this favorably ('slight increase'). Also, MaskGIT was trained 500k vs its original 2M steps, so the baseline may not be at its best.

The GroupSwap/data-dependent query mechanism seems underexplored: data-independent queries performed comparably (Table 5), and the parameter overhead is attributed to GroupSwap without a deeper analysis of why, leaving the architecture contribution feeling partially understood.
Writing polish issues (e.g., 'retaioning', 'while while', 'demonstrated can MGMs', 'perpleixty') and some typos in tables suggest the manuscript needed another editing pass.
